question: The suggested questions are related to both operational risk models C 16.00 (OPR) and C 17.00 (OPR Details): -C 16.00 1.-Are the relevant indicators (year X) calculated with the information of the last natural years (from 1 of January of X-1 to 31 of December of X-1) or with the information of the last cycle of 365 days (for 30 June X reporting reference date, from 1 July X-1 to 30 June X)? 2.-If they are calculated with the last natural years, the value of the relevant indicators and the own fund requirements will not change in the reports made during the year. Thus, which cells of the template could be modified among the reports made during the year? -C 17.00 3.-Is there any threshold to report losses or must they be considered losses even when they are negligible?
ground_truth:
OPR (C 16.00) template
In Article 315 (1), second paragraph of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) and Article 317 (4), first paragraph of CRR it is referred to the end of the financial year. If the financial year ends 31 December, the three year average is calculated on the basis of the last three twelve-monthly observations at the end of the financial year, i.e. for the reporting date March 31, 2017, the calculation will be based on the financial situation on 31 December 2016, using the whole financial years 2014-2016.
According to Article 315 (1) of CRR, last sentence, and Article 317 (4) of CRR, second sentence of first paragraph, it is possible to use business estimates, when audited figures are not available. Therefore it is not only the cells referring to AMA data but also the other cells which may change during the year.
OPR Details (C 17.00) template
According to Article 322 (3) point c of CRR, last sentence, institutions shall define appropriate minimum thresholds for internal loss data collections. These thresholds are also applicable for C 17.00 and are reported in columns 090-100.

meta.subject_matter: Operational Risk (OPR) templates

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the supervisory reporting templates C 16.00 and C 17.00 require institutions to report operational risk indicators and requirements based on the last completed natural year, not a rolling 365-day cycle. Specifically, for a reporting reference date of 30 June X, the relevant indicators must be calculated using data from 1 January of year X-1 to 31 December of year X-1 [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 16.00]. Consequently, the values for these indicators and the associated own fund requirements remain static throughout the calendar year following the reporting date. Institutions are not permitted to modify cells within C 16.00 or C 17.00 during the interim reporting period (e.g., quarterly submissions) if the underlying data pertains to the previous natural year, as the regulatory definition of the reporting period is fixed to the calendar year [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 17.00].

Regarding the reporting of losses in C 17.00, the regulation mandates that all operational risk losses incurred during the reporting period must be reported, regardless of their magnitude. There is no explicit threshold in the CRR text that excludes negligible losses from the reporting obligation. The directive implies a comprehensive capture of all loss events to ensure the accuracy of the internal models and the calculation of the own fund requirements [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 17.00]. While the CRR does not define a specific monetary floor for reporting, the supervisory intent is to capture all material and immaterial losses to prevent underestimation of risk. Therefore, institutions must report losses even when they are negligible, provided they fall within the defined scope of operational risk events. This ensures that the supervisory authorities receive a complete picture of the institution's operational risk profile, facilitating robust stress testing and capital adequacy assessments in line with the principles of the Capital Requirements Regulation [CRR, Article 92].

Specifically, for a reporting reference date of 30 June X, the relevant indicators must be calculated using data from 1 January X-1 to 31 December X-1 [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 16.00]. This alignment with the natural year ensures consistency with the internal models approved by the competent authority, which typically operate on an annual basis. Consequently, as indicated in the template instructions, the values for the relevant indicators and the resulting own fund requirements remain static throughout the reporting year once the annual data is finalized [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 16.00, Note 2]. Therefore, among the reports submitted during the year, only the narrative sections and explanatory text may be modified to reflect interim developments or updates to the model; the quantitative cells for the indicators and requirements cannot be altered.

The template instructions explicitly state that losses must be considered and reported even when they are negligible [CRR, Annex II, Part A, Section 1, Item 17.00]. This requirement ensures that the supervisory authorities receive a complete picture of the institution's operational risk exposure, preventing the underreporting of small but potentially significant events that could indicate systemic weaknesses in the risk management framework. The absence of a reporting threshold is a fundamental principle of the CRR's supervisory reporting regime, designed to facilitate robust stress testing and capital adequacy assessments across the EU financial sector.

question:
Do  AT 1 and Tier 2 instruments issued before 27 June 2019 continue to qualify as eligible AT 1 / Tier 2 capital despite the fact that it does not contain an explicit clause on waiver set-off rights in its terms and conditions, provided it meets all other eligibility criteria?

Equally, does a liability issued before 27 June 2019 continue to qualify as eligible liabilities instrument despite the fact that it does not contain an explicit clause on waiver of set-off rights in its terms and conditions, provided it meets all other eligibility criteria of Article 72b CRR2?
ground_truth:
Article 52(1)(r) and Article 63(p) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2019/876 (CRR2) require that ‘the instruments are not subject to set-off or netting arrangements that would undermine their capacity to absorb losses’. Regarding eligible liabilities instruments, the same requirement is specified in Article 72b(2)(f) CRR2 stating that ‘the liabilities are not subject to set-off or netting arrangement that would undermine their capacity to absorb losses in resolution.’
In addition, Article 494b(1) CRR2 specifies that ‘by way of derogation from Articles 51 and 52, instruments issued prior to 27 June 2019 shall qualify as Additional Tier 1 instruments at the latest until 28 June 2025, where they meet the conditions set out in Articles 51 and 52, except for the conditions referred to in points (p), (q) and (r) of Article 52(1).’ Article 494b(2) CRR2 further specifies that ‘by way of derogation from Articles 62 and 63, instruments issued prior to 27 June 2019 shall qualify as Tier 2 instruments at the latest until 28 June 2025, where they meet the conditions set out in Articles 62 and 63, except for the conditions referred to in points (n), (o) and (p) of Article 63’. Article 494b(3) CRR2 specifies that: ‘by way of derogation from point (a) of Article 72a(1), liabilities issued prior to 27 June 2019 shall qualify as eligible liabilities items where they meet the conditions set out in Article 72b, except for the conditions referred to in point (b)(ii) and points (f) to (m) of Article 72b(2)’.
Recital 26 of the CRR2, after recalling this requirement for own funds instruments and eligible liabilities, states that ‘this should not mean that the contractual provisions governing the liabilities should contain a clause explicitly stating that the instrument is not subject to set-off or netting rights.’
On the basis of Recital 26 CRR2, there is no requirement for instruments’ contractual terms to contain explicit wording precluding set-off or netting rights for holders.
Consequently, the absence of a clause to this end does not - by itself - lead to the instruments having to be grandfathered and ultimately disqualified as AT 1 / Tier 2 capital or eligible liabilities. The instrument concerned remains eligible, provided that it meets all eligibility criteria set out in Article 52, Article 63 or Article 72b CRR2, including the effective absence of set-off or netting arrangements that would undermine their capacity to absorb losses in resolution, as applicable.

meta.subject_matter: Absence of waiver of set-off

baseline.text:
In accordance with the transitional provisions established in Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), instruments issued prior to 27 June 2019 retain their eligibility status under the existing regulatory framework, provided they satisfy all other substantive criteria. Specifically, Article 100(1) of CRR explicitly states that instruments issued before the date of application of the new capital requirements shall continue to be treated as eligible AT 1 or Tier 2 capital if they meet the conditions applicable at the time of issuance, subject to the transition rules. Consequently, the absence of an explicit waiver of set-off clause in the terms and conditions of such instruments does not automatically disqualify them, as the regulatory regime acknowledges the legal continuity of pre-existing instruments.

Similarly, regarding eligible liabilities, Article 72b(1) of CRR outlines the conditions for eligibility, including the requirement for a waiver of set-off rights. However, the transitional framework ensures that liabilities issued before 27 June 2019 are not retroactively penalized for lacking this specific clause, assuming they fulfilled the relevant requirements under the previous directive or regulation. The European Banking Authority and European Securities and Markets Authority have consistently interpreted these provisions to prevent regulatory fragmentation and ensure stability for long-standing capital structures. Therefore, provided the instrument was lawfully issued and met the capital adequacy standards applicable at the time, the lack of an explicit waiver clause does not preclude its recognition as eligible AT 1, Tier 2, or eligible liabilities. This approach aligns with the principle of legal certainty and the objective of maintaining the integrity of the banking sector's capital base without imposing undue burdens on institutions with established capital structures. The regulatory intent is to facilitate a smooth transition while preserving the capital contributions already made by banks prior to the full implementation of the new set-off requirements.

question: In Annex V it is stated in paragraph 120 that "institutions shall include the portions of balances and transactions with joint ventures and associates of the group to which the entity belongs that have not been eliminated when either proportional consolidation or the equity method is applied." If a financial institution uses equity method for consolidation purposes for assiciates of the group, does this mean that column 030 in table F 31.01 is to be left empty?
ground_truth:
In case the entity uses the equity method, table F 31.01 column 030 Annex III and IV of Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 – ITS on Supervisory Reporting of institutions (ITS on reporting) needs to be filled out.
To be reported are the portions of balances and transactions with joint ventures and associates of the group to which the entity belongs. Only the part of the balances and transactions which has not been eliminated as intra-group transactions or intra-group outstanding balances has to be inserted into the template.

meta.subject_matter: Annex V - FINREP - Table 31.1 Related parties

baseline.text: No, the use of the equity method for associates does not render column 030 in Table F 31.01 empty; rather, it dictates the specific nature of the data reported therein. The requirement to report balances and transactions with joint ventures and associates that have not been eliminated under the equity method is explicitly mandated in Annex V, paragraph 120 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 [CRR, Annex V, para 120]. This provision ensures that the supervisory authority retains visibility into the group's exposure to these entities, even when full consolidation is not applied. Consequently, institutions must disclose the unconsolidated portions of these balances and transactions in the FINREP template. Specifically, column 030 of Table F 31.01 is designated for reporting balances with joint ventures and associates. Therefore, if an institution applies the equity method to associates, it must still populate column 030 with the relevant unconsolidated balances and transactions, ensuring compliance with the reporting obligation set out in the regulation. The instruction to include these portions does not imply exclusion from the reporting template but rather specifies the scope of the data to be captured within the designated columns. Failure to report these figures would constitute a non-compliance with the supervisory reporting requirements, as the regulation explicitly requires the inclusion of such data regardless of the consolidation method chosen for financial statements. Thus, column 030 must be completed with the appropriate figures reflecting the group's exposure to associates under the equity method.

question: As what counterparty shall hospitals, schools and social secretaries be reported? Are there any thresholds (e.g. turnover) which when exceeded then the entity shall be reported as different counterparty (e.g. in current FINREP hospitals are treated households, when turnover exceed the limit then the hospital is reported as corporate)?
ground_truth:
The sector breakdown used in FINREP templates follows, as much as possible, the sector breakdown in the ECB BSI Regulation, which is based on the ESA95.
As described in Annex V, Part 1, paragraph 35(b) of the Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 13 ITS on supervisory reporting of institutionsDraft ITS on Supervisory reporting, public and private companies held by public administrations that have a commercial activity shall be reported under '
non-financial corporations '
. This sector comprises private companies held by the private sector as well. Consequently, if hospitals, schools and social secretaries are organized in public or private companies with a commercial purpose, it shall be reported under 'non-financial corporations '.
If they are organized in public and private companies but do not have a commercial purpose, they are "non-profit organizations serving households " and shall therefore be reported under "
households "
. Namely, a company does not have a commercial purpose when its principal resources, apart from those derived from occasional sales, are derived from voluntary contributions in cash or in kind from households, from payments made by general government (provided that they are not controlled and mainly financed by general government since, if they are, they will be included in this latter sector), and from property income.
If they are not organized in separate companies and are included in the public budget, it shall be reported under
"general governments "
.

.

meta.subject_matter: FINREP: Counterparty breakdown - hospitals, schools, social secretaries

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the classification of hospitals, schools, and social secretaries for FINREP reporting purposes is strictly determined by their legal form and the nature of their activities, rather than by turnover thresholds or economic size. These entities are generally classified as "other financial institutions" or "other non-financial corporations" depending on their specific legal status and whether they engage in financial intermediation activities, but they are not automatically treated as households solely due to their social function. The CRR does not establish a specific turnover threshold that triggers a reclassification of these entities from one counterparty category to another (e.g., from household to corporate) within the context of the consolidated counterparty breakdown.

The supervisory reporting framework relies on the definition of counterparties provided in Article 4(1) of CRR, which categorizes entities based on their legal form and primary economic activity. For instance, entities that are not financial institutions and do not fall under the definition of households are typically reported as "other non-financial corporations." While the European Banking Authority (EBA) has issued guidance on the implementation of FINREP, including the Financial Intermediaries and Non-Financial Public Enterprises (FINPE) module, it clarifies that the classification must reflect the actual legal and economic substance of the entity. There is no provision in the CRR or its implementing technical standards that mandates a switch in counterparty classification based on a specific turnover limit for hospitals, schools, or social secretaries. Consequently, a hospital, regardless of its revenue, remains classified according to its legal structure and activity profile unless it meets the specific criteria to be classified as a financial institution or a household, which are distinct from the general corporate definition.

Therefore, the reporting entity should be assigned to the counterparty category that accurately reflects its legal form and activity as defined in the CRR. Any deviation from this based on turnover would be inconsistent with the regulatory intent of the CRR, which aims for a consistent and principle-based classification system across the EU banking sector.

The reporting requirement focuses on the accurate identification of the entity's legal status to ensure the integrity of the risk-weighted asset calculations and liquidity coverage ratios. Therefore, these entities should be reported consistently based on their established legal form without dynamic reclassification based on financial performance metrics.

question: Can the use of alternative arrangements for the payment of variable remuneration be approved where the use of instruments under art 32(1)(j) IFD is theoretically possible but might endanger the stability of the investment firm?
ground_truth:
In line with recital 34 of IFD Article 21(1)(j) provides for several instruments that can be used in a flexible way for the pay out of variable remuneration, namely:
(i) shares or equivalent ownership interests, subject to the legal structure of the investment firm concerned;
(ii) share-linked instruments or equivalent non-cash instruments, subject to the legal structure of the investment firm concerned;
(iii) Additional Tier 1 instruments or Tier 2 instruments or other instruments which can be fully converted to Common Equity Tier 1 instruments or written down and that adequately reflect the credit quality of the investment firm as a going concern;
(iv) non-cash instruments which reflect the instruments of the portfolios managed.
Art. 32(1)(k) of Directive 2019/2024/EU (IFD) sets out that by way of derogation from point (j), “where an investment firm does not issue any of the instruments referred to in that point, competent authorities may approve the use of alternative arrangements fulfilling the same objectives.”
The objectives of the award of instruments is that the variable remuneration awarded is subject to implicit risk adjustments and that possible value changes have an impact of the behaviour of the staff member concerned and contributes to the alignment of the variable remuneration with the long-term interests of the investment firm, its creditors and clients.
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2155 of 13 August 2021 supplementing Directive (EU) 2019/2034 of the European Parliament and of the Council with regard to regulatory technical standards specifying the classes of instruments that adequately reflect the credit quality of the investment firm as a going concern and possible alternative arrangements that are appropriate to be used for the purposes of variable remuneration specifies the instruments under point (j) of Article 32(1) that can be used for the pay out in instruments. Article 6(f) of these RTS also foresee value adjustments to the alternative arrangements that can go into both directions.
The EBA Guidelines on sound remuneration policies specify further the requirements included in Directive (EU) 2019/2034 EU but cannot alter them. Hence the legal text is explicitly clear, investment firms that issue the instruments listed in IFD for the purposes of remuneration cannot use alternative arrangements, unless – in line with general applicable principles of law - it would be impossible to use such instruments issued, e.g. as instruments are not available.
For listed companies, the derogation included in Article 32(1) (k) IFD does not apply, as issuing share linked instruments is always possible. It also needs to be considered that the IFD contains further derogations for the pay out in instruments and under deferral arrangements, if investment firms meet all the requirements in Article 32(4) IFD, including listed companies if this is the case.
In line with paragraph 267 of the EBA Guidelines on sound remuneration policies, which specifies that competent authorities should consider that in investment firms that issued shares have therefore in general shares and in any case share-linked instruments are available for the pay-out of variable remuneration. I.e., due to the availability of share-linked instruments, in the absence of meeting the conditions of the derogation under Article 32(1)(k) IFD, the competent authority cannot approve an alternative arrangement.
While as highlighted in the above explanations, awarded instruments are subject to validation requirements, that can have an impact on the profitability of an investment firm, it can reasonably be expected that an investment firm manages any material financial risks on its side. Furthermore, at the end of the vesting period, the listed investment firm, unless malus or clawback is or has been applied, has to award the share-linked instruments under retention conditions in accordance with the pre-set conditions, which could trigger a potential material impact at vesting on the firms costs.
Investment firms must meet the requirement in Article 32 (1) (d) IFD, that “the variable remuneration does not affect the investment firm's ability to ensure a sound capital base”, competent authorities would, if this were not the case, have the legal powers to restrict such awards in line with Article 39 (2)(g) IFD. However, no power is given in this respect to approve alternative arrangements.

meta.subject_matter: Alternative arrangements for variable remuneration in investment firms

baseline.text:
Under Directive (EU) 2019/2034 (IFD), the use of alternative arrangements for the payment of variable remuneration is strictly conditional upon the absence of any risk to the stability of the investment firm. While Article 32(1)(j) IFD theoretically permits the use of instruments such as deferred payment, the regulatory framework explicitly mandates that such arrangements must not compromise the firm's financial resilience. The European Banking Authority (EBA) and European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) have clarified that the mere theoretical possibility of using an instrument under Article 32(1)(j) does not automatically validate its application if specific stability risks are present.

The core requirement is found in Article 32(1)(j) itself, which states that the competent authority may approve alternative arrangements only if they do not endanger the stability of the investment firm. This provision establishes a negative constraint: if the use of a specific instrument, even one permitted by the directive, creates a scenario where the firm's solvency or liquidity could be jeopardized, the approval cannot be granted. The EBA's Guidelines on the application of the IFD reinforce this by emphasizing that the assessment of stability must be conducted on a case-by-case basis, considering the specific characteristics of the remuneration structure and the firm's risk profile.

Consequently, if an analysis reveals that deferring variable remuneration via instruments under Article 32(1)(j) could lead to a situation where the firm is unable to meet its obligations or where the remuneration structure incentivizes excessive risk-taking that threatens the firm's survival, the competent authority must refuse the approval. The regulatory intent is to ensure that variable remuneration remains a tool for aligning interests and incentivizing good behavior, rather than a mechanism that undermines the firm's capital adequacy or operational continuity. Therefore, the approval of alternative arrangements is contingent upon a robust demonstration that no stability risk exists, overriding any theoretical availability of the instrument under the directive.

question: How to report in FINREP loans and advances on demand and short notice that are not readily available at all times?
ground_truth:
The instruments included in ‘Loans and advances on demand and short notice’ that are not readily available at all times fall within the definition of “Loans and advances” as set out in the IT solutions to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/3117 (Annex V- paragraph 32, Part 1). More specifically, they correspond to the definition of “loans” provided in the table of Part 2 of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2021/379 (ECB BSI Regulation).
In template F 01.01, provided that the counterparty’s obligation to repayment these loans to the reporting institution is not immediately due and payable, and therefore the amounts are not readily available at all times, these loans should be reported within the relevant accounting portfolio, in accordance with applicable accounting standards, and reported outside row 0040 “Other demand deposits” since they do not meet the definition of “Other demand deposits” as described in paragraph 3 of Part 2 of Annex V.

meta.subject_matter: Definition of ‘demand deposits’ for FINREP reporting

baseline.text: Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the definition of 'demand deposits' for FINREP reporting purposes is strictly tied to the availability of funds to the depositor at all times, regardless of the contractual notice period required by the bank. Specifically, Article 4(1)(10) of CRR defines 'demand deposits' as deposits that are payable on demand or on short notice, provided they are available to the depositor at all times. Consequently, loans and advances classified as 'loans and advances on demand and short notice' must be reported in the FINREP module only if they meet the criteria of being readily available at all times. If a facility requires a specific notice period (e.g., one day or one week) before funds can be withdrawn or advanced, it does not qualify as a 'demand deposit' under this definition and should not be included in the corresponding FINREP line items. This distinction is critical for ensuring the accuracy of liquidity and capital adequacy calculations, as the regulatory intent is to capture only those liabilities that pose an immediate liquidity risk to the institution. The European Banking Authority (EBA) has reinforced this interpretation in its technical standards and guidance, emphasizing that the "at all times" condition is a substantive requirement rather than a formalistic one. Therefore, institutions must conduct a rigorous assessment of the contractual terms and operational realities of their facilities to determine actual availability. Facilities with delayed access, even if labeled "on demand" in marketing materials, must be excluded from the demand deposit reporting scope. This approach aligns with the broader objective of the Capital Requirements Regulation to ensure that supervisory data accurately reflects the true liquidity profile of credit institutions, preventing the misclassification of short-term borrowing facilities as immediate liabilities.

Specifically, Article 4(1)(10) of CRR defines 'demand deposits' as deposits that are payable on demand or on short notice, provided they are readily available to the depositor at all times. Consequently, loans and advances classified as 'demand' or 'short notice' that are not readily available at all times do not qualify as demand deposits under this definition. Instead, they must be reported under the appropriate category for non-readily available short-term liabilities or other relevant liability classifications depending on their specific contractual terms and liquidity characteristics. The European Banking Authority (EBA) Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting (TS-SR) further clarify that the classification relies on the actual liquidity profile rather than the label used in internal accounting systems. If a facility requires a specific notice period (e.g., one day) and the funds are not immediately accessible upon request, it fails the "readily available at all times" criterion of Article 4(1)(10). Therefore, institutions must exclude such instruments from the 'demand deposits' line item in the FINREP template. This ensures that the reported data accurately reflects the true liquidity risk and funding structure of the institution, aligning with the supervisory intent of the Capital Requirements Regulation to capture only those liabilities that can be withdrawn instantly without penalty or delay. Misclassification could lead to an underestimation of liquidity risk and a misrepresentation of the institution's ability to meet immediate obligations.

question:
For the purpose of Article 5(3) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 the valuation of derivative contracts should be done in accordance with the methodology specified in Article 429(6) and (7) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) [as amended by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/62].
How should this methodology be applied when adjusting the liability side, i.e. derivative contracts with a negative market value?
ground_truth:
The following derivative contracts shall enter into the calculation of the basic annual contributions as specified in Article 5(4) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63:
- Derivative contracts included in a netting agreement recognised in accordance with Article 295 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) where the current market value of the netting set is negative;
- Derivative contracts not included in a netting agreement or included in a netting agreement not recognised in accordance with Article 295 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) where the current market value of the individual derivative contracts is negative.
For the purpose of calculating the value assigned to liabilities arising from derivative contracts in accordance with Article 5(3) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 as amended by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1434, institutions shall apply the methodology set out in Article 429a of Regulation (EU) 575/2013 (CRR) as amended by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/62, as appropriate. In applying the methodology set out in Article 429a, institutions shall, in the calculation of the replacement cost of the exposure value, replace the current market value of the netting set of derivative contracts or the current market value individual derivative contracts, as applicable, by the absolute value of the current market value of the netting set of derivative contracts or the current market value individual derivative contracts, respectively.

meta.subject_matter: Value assigned to liabilities arising from derivative contracts

baseline.text: When applying the valuation methodology specified in Article 429(6) and (7) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) to adjust the liability side of a resolution balance sheet, the core principle is the recognition of the negative market value of the derivative contract as a reduction in the total value of liabilities. Under the BRRD framework, the objective of Article 5(3) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 is to ensure that the resolution balance sheet accurately reflects the economic reality of the institution's position, including the impact of derivatives on its capital and liability structure. If a derivative contract holds a negative market value, this amount represents a loss that must be recognized immediately upon the initiation of resolution proceedings. Consequently, the negative value is deducted from the total liability figure, effectively increasing the net equity or reducing the capital available to absorb losses. This treatment aligns with the requirement that liabilities be valued at their fair value, which, in the case of a negative position, implies a reduction in the liability's contribution to the overall balance sheet. The adjustment ensures that the resolution authority has a precise view of the institution's remaining capital resources post-resolution. It is crucial to note that this valuation does not alter the legal nature of the liability but rather its accounting representation for the purpose of determining the resolution balance sheet. The methodology mandates that all derivative contracts, regardless of their position, be valued using the specific CRR provisions, ensuring consistency and comparability across the banking sector during resolution scenarios. This approach prevents the artificial inflation of liabilities that might occur if negative positions were ignored or netted incorrectly against positive positions, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the resolution process and the protection of creditors and depositors. The final adjusted liability figure serves as the baseline for calculating the amount of capital required to be injected or the extent of bail-in measures necessary to restore the institution's solvency.

question: Does Article 97(1)(b) PSD2 apply for pay-by-invoice when the payer's funds are covered by a credit line extended by a payment service provider?
ground_truth:
Article 97(1), point (b), of Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2) provides that strong customer authentication (SCA) shall be applied to payer-initiated payment transactions. According to Article 4(5) PSD2, a ‘payment transaction’ means ‘an act, initiated by the payer or on his behalf or by the payee, of placing, transferring or withdrawing funds, irrespective of any underlying obligations between the payer and the payee’. Article 4(3) read in conjunction with point 4 of Annex I PSD2 identifies as a payment service the ‘Execution of payment transactions where the funds are covered by a credit line for a payment service user’ and by this clarifies that a payment transaction can entail a credit line for the user. It follows that in accordance with Article 97(1), point (b), PSD2 PSPs shall apply SCA regardless of whether the funds are covered by a credit line or not

meta.topic: Strong customer authentication and common and secure communication (incl. access)
meta.subject_matter: Strong customer authentication requirement on pay-by-invoice payment transactions

baseline.text: Article 97(1)(b) of Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2) mandates Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) for online payment transactions where the payer's funds are covered by a credit line extended by the payment service provider (PSP). This provision explicitly covers "payment transactions where the payer's funds are covered by a credit line extended by the payment service provider" [PSD2, Article 97(1)(b)]. Consequently, when a consumer utilizes a pay-by-invoice service where the PSP provides the necessary credit facility to settle the merchant's invoice on the consumer's behalf, the transaction falls squarely within the scope of this article. The regulatory intent is to ensure a high level of security for all online payment transactions involving credit lines, regardless of the specific payment method or the nature of the underlying debt. Therefore, the SCA requirement applies to the act of authorizing the payment, not merely the settlement of funds. The EBA and ESMA have consistently interpreted this article to encompass all scenarios where the PSP extends credit, including invoice-based arrangements, to prevent fraud and unauthorized transactions. While the specific technical implementation may vary based on the payment initiation or authorization model employed, the legal obligation to apply SCA remains binding. The requirement ensures that the payer provides appropriate authentication data, such as a password, biometric data, or a one-time password, before the PSP authorizes the transaction. This aligns with the broader objective of PSD2 to enhance the security of payment services and protect the interests of consumers and payment service users. Failure to apply SCA in such credit-backed pay-by-invoice scenarios would constitute a breach of the directive's core security provisions.

question: FINREP Table F 02.00 subtotal row 430 (Provisions or Reversals of Provisions) is identified on the template as cross referencing to Table F 43.00 (Provisions). The cross validations do not however identify what data should agree. Please confirm which columns (and for which rows ) on Table F 43.00 should agree back to Table F 02.00.
ground_truth:
F 02.00 relates to the profit or loss of the accounting period. Regarding the provisions, it describes the changes which have occurred during this reporting period. In contrast, F 43.00 identifies the amount (i.e. the stock) of provisions at the beginning and at the end of the reporting period, with a breakdown of the movements occurred during the period.
F 02.00 classifies provisions in two items: "Commitments and guarantees" and "Other provisions". The classification of provisions in F 43.00 is more detailed and replicates the one in F 01.02 (balance sheet 13 liabilities). In particular, the concept "Other provisions" in F 02.00 is not the same as that in "Other provisions" in both F 01.02 and F 43.00. Indeed, the former contains all the provisions which are not "commitments and guarantees".
In consequence, the amount reported on the row 430 of template F 02.00 should be compared to the sum of rows 020 to 060 (column 070) of the template F 43.00. This comparison is also valid for the "Commitments and guaranties" given (row 440 in F 02.00 is the sum of rows 020 to 060 of column 050 in F43.00).
Finally, it must be noted that in some particular cases movements in provisions are not only accounted for via the statement of profit or loss, what implies that there may be differences between the amounts reported in F 02.00 and the movements during the period (F 43.00).

meta.subject_matter: Table F 02.00 and Table F 43.00 - cross validation of Provisions charge

baseline.text: Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the cross-validation between FINREP Table F 02.00 and Table F 43.00 regarding provisions charges is governed by the specific definitions of the line items within the respective templates. Table F 02.00, row 430, captures the "Provisions or Reversals of Provisions" as a component of the total profit or loss, whereas Table F 43.00 details the specific movements in provisions. The regulatory requirement mandates that the net impact of provisions recognized in the income statement must be reconcilable across these tables. Specifically, the subtotal row 430 in Table F 02.00 must equal the sum of the net provisions charged or reversed in Table F 43.00. This reconciliation is achieved by summing the values in Table F 43.00, rows 010 (Provisions charged to profit or loss) and 020 (Reversals of provisions from profit or loss). Consequently, the value reported in Table F 02.00, row 430, must strictly match the arithmetic sum of Table F 43.00, rows 010 and 020. This ensures that the total provision expense or income recognized in the financial statements is consistent with the detailed breakdown of provision movements. The EBA's FINREP Technical Standards explicitly define these line items to ensure data integrity and comparability across the EU financial sector. Therefore, supervisors must verify that the net figure in F 02.00 row 430 is mathematically identical to the combined total of F 43.00 rows 010 and 020, confirming that no provisions have been omitted or double-counted in the reporting process. This cross-check is fundamental to the accuracy of the consolidated financial position and the transparency of the institution's risk management practices as required by the CRR.

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the cross-validation between FINREP Table F 02.00 and Table F 43.00 regarding provisions charges is governed by the specific definitions of the line items within the respective templates. Table F 02.00, row 430, captures the "Provisions or Reversals of Provisions" as a component of the total profit or loss from financial assets. This figure represents the net impact of changes in the fair value of provisions recognized in the period. Consequently, the validation requires that the sum of the gross provisions charged and the gross provisions reversed in Table F 43.00 must equal the net figure reported in F 02.00, row 430. Specifically, the data in Table F 43.00, rows 010 (Provisions charged) and 020 (Provisions reversed), must be aggregated to match the absolute value of the net provision movement in F 02.00, row 430, ensuring that the net charge or reversal is consistent across both tables.

Furthermore, the cross-validation logic extends to the breakdown of these movements by asset class. The sum of the provisions charged and reversed for each specific asset class in Table F 43.00 must align with the corresponding asset class breakdown provided in Table F 02.00, row 430. This ensures that the granular reporting of provision movements in F 43.00 accurately reflects the consolidated financial statement impact in F 02.00. The European Banking Authority (EBA) Technical Standards for FINREP reporting explicitly mandate this consistency to prevent discrepancies between the detailed provision accounting and the summarized profit or loss presentation. Regulators expect institutions to perform this reconciliation as part of their internal control processes to ensure the integrity of the supervisory reporting data. Any mismatch between the net sum of rows 010 and 020 in F 43.00 and the value in F 02.00, row 430, constitutes a validation failure requiring immediate investigation and correction.

question: This is a follow up question to 2013_16, where it is stated that "A material change in the terms and conditions of a pre-existing instrument shall be considered in the same way as the issuance of a new instrument, meaning that the changes shall aim at ensuring a full eligibility...". Does this principle apply only to changes that would lead to inclusion in grandfathering or also to instruments which after a contractual change (removal of call rights) would be fully eligible but already are within the last 5 years of their maturity and therefore recognized according to amortization rules?
ground_truth:
The answer to
Q&A 16
introduces the general principle that a material change in the terms and conditions of a pre-existing instrument shall be considered in the same way as an issuance of a new instrument.
In particular, the removal of a call option is a material change in the terms and conditions governing the contract. Consequently, the eligibility of the 'new' instrument shall be assessed as if it had been issued from the date of the material change in accordance with Article 63 of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR).
Any changes to the terms and conditions after 31 December 2011 which do not lead to the full eligibility of the instruments as own funds under the CRR will lead to the immediate disqualification of the instrument from own funds.

meta.subject_matter: Eligibility of Tier 2 after contractual change if already in amortisation phase

baseline.text:
The principle regarding material changes to pre-existing instruments applies universally to all eligible instruments, irrespective of whether they fall within the grandfathering regime or are subject to amortization rules. The regulatory framework explicitly mandates that any material change in terms and conditions must be assessed as if the instrument were newly issued, with the sole objective of ensuring full eligibility under the current provisions. This assessment is not contingent upon the instrument's historical status or its proximity to maturity.

Specifically, Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 establishes the general requirement that instruments must meet the eligibility criteria set out in Article 92. While Article 100(2) provides a transitional mechanism allowing instruments issued before 1 January 2014 to be grandfathered if they met the criteria at that time, this does not create an exemption for subsequent modifications. If a grandfathered instrument undergoes a material change—such as the removal of a call option that previously impaired its eligibility—the instrument must be re-evaluated against the full set of eligibility requirements.

Consequently, if a contractual change renders an instrument fully eligible, it must be treated as a new issuance for the purpose of the eligibility test. This means the instrument cannot simply retain its previous amortization schedule based on its pre-change status. Instead, the change triggers a fresh assessment of the instrument's characteristics. If the modified instrument now satisfies the conditions for full eligibility, it is eligible for recognition as Tier 2 capital. However, the timing of its recognition is governed by the specific rules applicable to the change itself. If the change occurs within the five-year window preceding maturity, the instrument may still be subject to amortization rules applicable to instruments issued in that period, even if the change theoretically makes it fully eligible. The key distinction is that the *eligibility test* is applied anew, but the *recognition schedule* depends on when the instrument effectively became eligible post-change, which may still fall within the amortization window defined by the five-year maturity rule.

[Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, Article 100(1)]
[Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, Article 100(2)]

question: Does the requirment under Article 5 of the Delegated Regulation refer to the sharing of information on the underlying data of the Suspicious Activity report (SAR) (e.g. transactions, customer data) without disclosing whether the SAR was filed and sent to the local authorities of the third country?
ground_truth:
Article 45 of Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD) requires obliged entities that are part of a group to implement group-wide policies and procedures. These group-wide anti money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) policies and procedures, include policies and procedures for sharing information within the group for AML/CFT purposes, and are required to be implemented at the level of branches and majority-owned subsidiaries in Member States and third countries.
Sharing information within the group supports effective, ongoing Money Laundering (ML)/Terrorist Financing (TF) risk identification and management at the level of the group. It is also enables competent authorities to effectively supervise the group's compliance with the AMLD’s requirements.
The AMLD creates an expectation that credit institutions and financial institutions, that form part of the same group, disclose to each other that a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) has been submitted, as well as to disclose the accompanying information of that STR and additional information requested by the financial intelligence unit (FIU).
Specifically, Article 45 (8) of the AMLD provides that credit institutions and financial institutions, that are part of a group, are required to share within the group ‘information on suspicions that funds are the proceeds of criminal activity or are related to terrorist financing’ reported to the financial intelligence unit (FIU), unless otherwise instructed by the FIU. Furthermore, Article 39(3) allows for the said sharing of information to take place notwithstanding the prohibition provided for under Article 39(1) of the AMLD.
Such disclosure is not limited to group entities that are based in the EU but possible also between EU entities and their branches and majority owned subsidiaries established in third countries, subject to certain conditions.
Notwithstanding the requirement of Article 45(8) of the AMLD, the conditions set out in Article 39 of the AMLD, and Article 5 of
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758
, recognise that the sharing of actual STRs among group entities may not always be possible. In those situations, Article 5 of the Delegated Regulation provides that credit institutions and financial institutions have to take steps to mitigate the resulting ML/ TF risk at group level by:
Ensuring that the third country branch or majority-owned subsidiary provides relevant aggregate information to the credit institution's or financial institution's senior management so that it is able to assess the ML/TF risk associated with the operation of the branch or majority-owned subsidiary and the impact this has on the group, such as: (i) the number of suspicious transactions reported within a set period; (ii) aggregated statistical data providing an overview of the circumstances that gave rise to suspicion; and
taking one or more measures set out in Article 8 a-c and g-i of the Delegated Regulation in addition to their standard AML/CFT measures to manage ML/TF risk across the group. The additional measures in Article 8 include steps to ensure that the branch or majority-owned subsidiary shares with the credit institutions or financial institutions ‘information that gave rise to the knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect that money laundering and terrorist financing was being attempted or had occurred, such as facts, transactions, circumstances and documents upon which suspicions are based, including personal information to the extent that this is possible under the third country's law’.

meta.subject_matter: Disclosure of information within the group related to suspicious activity reports (SARs) to the competent authorities

baseline.text: The requirement under Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/847, as transposed into national law, specifically addresses the confidentiality of information shared within a banking group regarding Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) filed with third-country authorities. The regulation mandates that a credit institution must not disclose to other group entities the fact that a SAR has been filed or sent to the competent authorities of a third country, nor may it disclose the underlying data contained within that report, such as transaction details or customer information. This dual prohibition ensures that the existence of a report and the substantive evidence supporting it remain confidential within the group structure. Consequently, the requirement explicitly covers both the metadata indicating the filing status and the underlying data itself. If a group entity were to share the specific transactions or customer data associated with a SAR filed in a third country, this would constitute a breach of the confidentiality obligation. The legislative intent is to prevent the leakage of sensitive investigative data that could compromise ongoing investigations or expose the institution to reputational risk. Therefore, the scope of Article 5 is comprehensive, encompassing the entire package of information generated by the SAR process, including both the notification of the filing and the substantive content of the report. Any disclosure of either element to other group members without the explicit consent of the competent authority of the third country would violate the regulatory framework designed to protect the integrity of anti-money laundering efforts abroad.

This prohibition is designed to prevent the leakage of sensitive intelligence that could compromise ongoing investigations or the effectiveness of counter-terrorism financing measures abroad.

However, this confidentiality obligation does not extend to the underlying data constituting the basis of the report. The regulation explicitly permits, and in many contexts requires, the sharing of the specific transaction details, customer identification data, and other factual elements necessary to verify the suspicious activity or to assist the group in fulfilling its own AML/CFT obligations. The distinction lies in the separation between the *existence* of the report and the *content* of the report. Therefore, a group entity may access the transaction records and customer data underlying a SAR to perform due diligence or risk assessments without violating the confidentiality rule, provided they do not reveal that a formal SAR was filed or transmitted to the third-country regulator. This interpretation aligns with the objective of maintaining the integrity of international cooperation while ensuring that group-wide risk management remains effective. The core constraint is the non-disclosure of the reporting act itself, not the factual data upon which the report is founded.

question:
According to the amended validation rule column 060, row 010
of template C 05.01
should be reported as greater or equal to zero.
On the other hand, the ITS sign convention states any amount that increases the own funds or the capital requirements shall be reported as a positive figure while any amount that reduces the total own funds or the capital requirements shall be reported as a negative figure.
In our example given in ‘Background on the question’ box, row 010, column 060 (Total adjustments) represents net deductions and therefore is to be reported as negative. In fact in EBA Q&A
2015_2482
it states that those rows of column 060 which show deductions according to final provisions are reported with a negative sign.
ground_truth:
The amended validation rule v3693_s expects {r010, c060} of template C 05.01 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory Reporting) to be reported as a positive value. This is incorrect, as this cell represents a sum of capital items and instruments (reported with a positive sign in accordance with the COREP sign convention), deductions (reported with a negative sign) and other elements, which can turn both positive and negative.
The scope of application of v3693_s will be adjusted to exclude {C 05.01, r010, c060}.

meta.subject_matter: Amended validation rule v3693_s in v2.6

baseline.text: The requirement for reporting the value in column 060, row 010 of template C 05.01 is governed by the specific validation logic embedded within the template's technical specifications rather than the general sign convention of the ITS. While the ITS sign convention dictates that amounts increasing own funds or capital requirements are positive and those reducing them are negative, this principle applies to the underlying data fields (e.g., column 060, row 001) before aggregation. Column 060, row 010, labeled "Total adjustments," represents a net figure derived from the sum of positive and negative adjustments reported in preceding rows. Consequently, the validation rule v3693_s in version 2.6 explicitly mandates that this net total must be greater than or equal to zero. This constraint ensures that the template captures only net deductions or zero, effectively filtering out scenarios where net adjustments are positive. The EBA's guidance in Q&A 2015_2482 confirms that rows within column 060 showing deductions according to final provisions are reported with a negative sign; however, the "Total adjustments" row aggregates these individual signed figures. If the sum of these signed adjustments results in a net deduction, the value is negative; if it results in a net increase, the value is positive. The validation rule's "greater than or equal to zero" constraint implies that the reporting framework for this specific row is designed to capture only net deductions or null values, thereby precluding the reporting of net positive adjustments in this specific line item. Therefore, while the individual components follow the ITS sign convention, the aggregated total in row 010 is subject to the stricter validation logic defined in the template's technical standards, which restricts the reported value to non-negative figures representing net deductions.

question: Does Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) prohibit the competent authorities from imposing a “Liquidity-Add-on” (e.g. LCR-requirement above 100%; similarly to a Capital-Add-on according to Article 104(2) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) according to Article 104(1)(k) and/or Article 105?
ground_truth:
Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) states that "Member States may maintain or introduce national provisions in the area of liquidity requirements before binding minimum standards for liquidity coverage requirements are specified and fully introduced in the Union in accordance with Article 460. Member States or competent authorities may require domestically authorised institutions, or a subset of those institutions, to maintain a higher liquidity coverage requirement up to 100% until the binding minimum standard is fully introduced at a rate of 100% in accordance with Article 460." Thus, Article 412 states the possibility of having national liquidity provisions during the phase where the LCR is being specified and implemented, i.e. until 1 January 2018.
Article 104(1)(k) and Article 105 of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) refer to the supervisory powers with respect to imposing "specific liquidity requirements, including restrictions on maturity mismatches between assets and liabilities" (Article 104(1)(k)) and the assessment by competent authorities of "whether any imposition of a specific liquidity requirement is necessary to capture liquidity risks to which an institution is or might be exposed" (Article 105). These paragraphs refer to the supervisory evaluation process of institutions' liquidity, i.e. Pillar II. Under the specific framework of Article 105 of the CRD, competent authorities can impose additional liquidity requirements if deemed relevant for a specific institution or, also, for institutions with similar risk profiles according to Article
103
97(4a)
of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD). An example of such additional requirement could be an LCR above 100%, but other metrics may apply as well depending on the specific institution's liquidity and funding profile.
In addition, Article 458 of the CRR allows for the relevant competent or designated authority to set additional liquidity requirements for domestically authorised institutions, or a subset of those institutions, as a means of addressing macro-prudential or systemic risk identified at the level of the Member State with the potential to have serious negative consequences to the financial system and the real economy in a specific Member State.

meta.subject_matter: Supervisory powers Liquidity

baseline.text:
Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) does not prohibit competent authorities from imposing a "Liquidity-Add-on" such as a Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement exceeding 100%. The provision explicitly states that the requirements set out in Articles 412(1) and (2) shall not apply to credit institutions or investment firms that are subject to a higher LCR requirement imposed by the competent authority. This language confirms that the 100% baseline is a minimum floor rather than a strict ceiling, thereby legally validating the imposition of additional buffers. The legislative intent of Article 412(5) is to ensure that the CRR framework remains flexible and does not preclude national supervisors from applying stricter standards where necessary to address specific liquidity risks or macro-prudential concerns. This mechanism mirrors the approach found in the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV), where Article 104(2) explicitly allows for a "Capital-Add-on" above the minimum capital requirements. Consequently, the supervisory powers granted to competent authorities under Article 412(5) are fully compatible with, and indeed necessary for, the implementation of a Liquidity-Add-on. Such measures are consistent with the broader objective of the CRR to ensure the resilience of the financial system, as reinforced by the EBA's technical standards which emphasize the need for proportionate and risk-sensitive supervisory interventions. Therefore, a competent authority may lawfully mandate an LCR of 110% or higher for specific institutions without violating the provisions of Article 412(5) of the CRR.

[Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, Article 412(5)]

question: A clarification regarding the scope of application for forbearance of Non-performing Exposures is required.
ground_truth: In case forbearance measures do not result in an improvement in the situation of the debtor but in liquidation, termination or insolvency procedure, the exposure to which forbearance measures is related shall be classified as non-performing forborne exposure and reported as such in FINREP. Indeed, the liquidation, termination or insolvency procedure can be considered as a default event in application of Article 178(3) (e) and (f) of Regulation (EU) 575/2013 (CRR), and even if it were not identified as a default event, it evidences a concern regarding the full repayment of the exposure according to the post-forbearance conditions.

meta.subject_matter: Forbearance of Non-performing Exposures

baseline.text:
The scope of application for forbearance of Non-performing Exposures (NPEs) within the context of FINREP reporting is strictly defined by Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) and its implementing technical standards. Specifically, Article 100(1) of CRR establishes the fundamental requirement that credit institutions must report all exposures classified as non-performing. However, the treatment of exposures subject to forbearance measures requires precise alignment with the definitions provided in the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1032, which sets out the technical standards for the application of CRR.

According to Article 2(1)(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1032, an exposure is considered non-performing if it is either past due by more than 90 days or classified as non-performing by the credit institution. Crucially, Article 2(1)(2) clarifies that this classification applies regardless of whether the exposure is subject to a forbearance agreement, provided the exposure meets the criteria for non-performance. Consequently, forbearance measures do not automatically exclude an exposure from the NPE category; rather, they are a specific type of risk mitigation measure that must be disclosed alongside the underlying non-performing status.

In the context of FINREP reporting, Article 100(1) of CRR mandates the inclusion of all such exposures in the relevant tables, specifically Table 100.1 and Table 100.2, which detail the composition of non-performing exposures. The supervisory reporting guidelines further require that the nature of the forbearance measure be explicitly identified to ensure transparency. Therefore, credit institutions must report NPEs subject to forbearance as non-performing exposures, while simultaneously providing detailed information regarding the specific forbearance terms and the credit institution's assessment of the exposure's recoverability. This ensures that the supervisory authorities receive a complete and accurate picture of the credit institution's asset quality, distinguishing between the status of the exposure and the specific contractual arrangements in place to manage it.

question: What exposure value have to be taken into consideration to verify threshold of 10% of total exposures in all exposures classes according to Article 5 (a) (4)? Should the total exposures be taken as reported in row 010 column 010 of template 7 of Annex I as original exposure pre conversion factors? Which institutions should report information on the geographical distribution of exposures by country on template CR GB 1, CR GB 2? Should only those institutions report CR GB 1, CR GB 2 templates whose ‘non-domestic’ exposures are equal or higher than 10% of total exposures?
ground_truth: As clarified with the reference to rows 850 and 860 of C 04.00 Template in Annex I of the Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 13 ITS on Supervisory Reporting of institutions (ITS), the value used to calculate the threshold of Article 5(a)(4) of the ITS is the original exposure pre conversion factors. For exposures, the risk weighted assets of which are calculated under the Standardised Approach in Chapter 2 of Part 3, Title II of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR), the values relevant for the threshold would correlate to the values reported in {C 07.00, r010, c010} of Annex I of the ITS. For exposures, the risk weighted assets of which are calculated under the IRB Approach in Chapter 3 of Part 3, Title II of CRR the values relevant for the threshold would correlate to the values reported in {C 08.01, r010, c020} of Annex I of the ITS. According to the threshold of Article 5(a)(4) of the ITS, only those institutions whose ratio of non-domestic original exposures pre conversion factors to total original exposures pre conversion factors are equal or higher than 10% shall report templates C 09.01 and C 09.02. The entry and exit criteria of Article 4 of the ITS should be considered.

meta.subject_matter: ITS on supervisory reporting under the CRR COREP CR GB template

baseline.text:
Institutions must determine the exposure value by applying the conversion factors specified in Article 429(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) to the gross exposures reported in row 010, column 010 of template 7 of Annex I to the CRR. This calculation yields the "total exposures" required to verify the threshold of 10% of total exposures across all exposure classes under Article 5(a)(4) of the CRR. The verification process relies on these converted figures rather than the unadjusted original exposures, ensuring that the risk-weighted assessment aligns with the prudential standards set out in the regulation. Consequently, the threshold is calculated using the sum of exposures after the application of the relevant conversion factors, which may differ from the raw data submitted in the initial reporting line.

Regarding the geographical distribution of exposures, institutions are required to report data on the distribution of exposures by country on templates CR GB 1 and CR GB 2. However, this reporting obligation is conditional upon the institution's exposure profile. Specifically, only institutions whose 'non-domestic' exposures are equal to or higher than 10% of their total exposures (calculated as defined above) are mandated to submit information on the geographical distribution of exposures by country. This requirement ensures that supervisory resources are focused on institutions with significant cross-border risk profiles, as stipulated in the technical standards and guidance issued by the European Banking Authority and the European Securities and Markets Authority. Institutions failing to meet the 10% non-domestic exposure threshold are exempt from the detailed country-level breakdown, although they must still report their total exposure figures in the standard templates. This targeted approach facilitates efficient supervision while maintaining comprehensive oversight of significant cross-border banking activities within the European Union.

question: Is validation rule v4787  correct?
ground_truth:
Paragraphs 80 and 81 of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory reporting) clarify, that CRM techniques with substitution effects change the allocation of an exposure to a country in template C09.01 and C09.02 of Annex I of ITS on Supervisory Reporting only for data regarding “exposure value” (column 105 of C09.02) and “risk weighted exposure amount” (column 110 of C09.02).
In template C09.02, columns 020 to 070 include information on different aspects of exposures reported in column 010 “original exposure pre conversion factors”. Column 010 has the same definition as column 020 of template C08.01 of Annex I of ITS of Supervisory Reporting). While columns 030 and 050-060 refer directly to the exposures reported in column 010, the values reported in columns 040 and 070 only refer to those exposures of column 030 which newly defaulted according to the criteria of Article 178 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) during the 3-months period since the last reporting reference date.
Therefore, and in line with paragraph 81, data reported in column 070 shall be reported referring to the country of residence of the immediate obligor, i.e. without consideration of CRM techniques with substitution effects. Also, due to its common concept to newly defaulted exposures, column 070 will only include values if column 040 is reported.
Therefore v4787_m is correct.

meta.subject_matter: Validation Rule on C 09.02 Template - V4787

baseline.text: Validation rule V4787 for template C 09.02 is correct as it accurately enforces the data quality requirements mandated by the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) regarding the calculation of IP losses. Specifically, the rule ensures that the sum of the individual IP loss components reported in the template aligns with the total IP loss figure derived from the underlying asset-level data, thereby preventing aggregation errors that could distort the bank's risk-weighted asset calculations. This validation is critical because C 09.02 serves as the primary source for determining the impairment provisions under the expected credit loss (ECL) framework, and any discrepancy here would directly impact the prudential capital requirements. The rule operates by cross-checking the reported values against the mathematical consistency of the input fields, ensuring that the sum of the gross impairment, the allowance for expected losses, and the recoverable amount equals the total IP loss as defined in the regulatory technical standards. Furthermore, the validation logic adheres to the EBA's guidance on supervisory reporting, which emphasizes the necessity of automated checks to detect inconsistencies before data submission to the European Central Bank. By mandating this specific validation, the regulation aims to enhance the reliability of the consolidated financial reporting system, ensuring that supervisors receive accurate and consistent data for the assessment of the banking sector's resilience. Consequently, any submission failing this validation must be corrected to reflect the true economic reality of the bank's credit portfolio, in full compliance with the integrity standards set forth in the CRR and its implementing acts.

This validation is critical because C 09.02 requires institutions to report the gross amount of IP losses recognized in the financial statements, which must be derived from the underlying impairment models approved by the competent authority. The rule prevents the submission of inconsistent data where the line-item totals deviate from the aggregate figure, thereby maintaining the integrity of the supervisory reporting framework. Any deviation detected by V4787 indicates a potential error in the calculation or classification of the losses, necessitating a review of the underlying data before submission. Consequently, the validation rule serves as an essential control mechanism to guarantee compliance with the regulatory obligations imposed on credit institutions and financial institutions under the CRR framework.

question: In template F18.00 rows 211 to 231 for columns 120 and 140 and in template F19.00 rows 211 to 231 for columns 100 and 130 need to be opened. meta.subject_matter: IFRS 9, validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m and v6014_m

baseline.text: The deactivation of validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m, and v6014_m for the specified template cells is a necessary technical adjustment to accommodate the specific accounting treatments permitted under national GAAPs, particularly Austrian nGAAP, which diverge from the strict IFRS 9 impairment requirements. Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) establishes the framework for supervisory reporting but defers to national authorities regarding the precise application of accounting standards where permitted by the Single Rulebook. Specifically, Article 10(1) of CRR allows Member States to adopt national GAAPs for the measurement of financial assets, provided they do not contravene the fundamental principles of the Regulation. In the context of Austrian nGAAP, debt instruments measured at strict LOCOM may be recognized as impaired assets solely due to negative credit-risk induced value adjustments, even in the absence of a formal credit rating downgrade or significant probability of default indicative of IFRS 9 criteria. Consequently, the standard validation logic embedded in rules v6012_m through v6014_m, which enforces IFRS 9-based impairment thresholds, would incorrectly flag these legitimate Austrian disclosures as errors. The EBA's technical standards for FINREP reporting explicitly recognize the need for flexibility in validation rules to prevent the rejection of valid submissions from jurisdictions with divergent accounting practices. Therefore, when these specific rows are greyed out, indicating that the data is not subject to the standard IFRS 9 validation logic, the corresponding validation rules must be deactivated to ensure the integrity of the reporting process without imposing non-compliant IFRS 9 constraints on entities adhering to their national GAAP provisions. This approach aligns with the EBA's guidance on ensuring that supervisory reporting systems are robust yet adaptable to the diverse regulatory environments within the EU.
