Under MiFID II, a person who is not authorised as an investment firm but satisfies the conditions set out in Article 53(3) of Directive 2014/65/EU is legally permitted to act as a member or participant of a regulated market or a Multilateral Trading Facility (MTF). Article 53(3) explicitly defines such an entity as an "unauthorised person" that meets specific criteria, including being a financial institution authorised in a third country or a financial market operator authorised in a third country, provided they comply with the relevant third-country regulations and are subject to supervision by a competent authority in that third country [Directive 2014/65/EU, Article 53(3)].

The regulatory framework distinguishes between authorised investment firms and these unauthorised persons regarding their capacity to participate in organised trading venues. While Article 4(1)(a) generally requires investment firms to be authorised to provide investment services, Article 53(3) creates a specific exemption for unauthorised persons meeting the aforementioned criteria, allowing them to engage in activities that would otherwise be restricted [Directive 2014/65/EU, Article 53(3)]. Consequently, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the European Banking Authority (EBA) have clarified in their technical standards and guidance that the definition of a "member" or "participant" under Articles 26 and 27 of the Directive encompasses both authorised investment firms and unauthorised persons falling within the scope of Article 53(3) [ESMA/2017/100, ESMA/2017/101].

This permission is contingent upon the unauthorised person adhering to the conduct of business rules and transparency requirements applicable to members of regulated markets or MTFs, as outlined in Articles 26 and 27 respectively. Furthermore, the unauthorised person must ensure that their activities do not undermine the integrity of the market or the protection of investors, maintaining the same level of regulatory oversight as authorised entities within the EU framework. Therefore, the legal status of being an unauthorised person under Article 53(3) does not preclude membership in organised trading venues, provided all statutory conditions are strictly met.

question: For application of the grandfathering rules defined in Article 484 CRR and following, does the change in debtor resulting from a merger means that a new capital instrument has been issued and that its eligibility for grandfathering or for full eligibility as an own fund instrument should be assessed at the date of the merger or should one use the initial characteristics of the bond?
ground_truth:
As specified in
Q&A 2013_16
, changes made to pre-CRR instruments shall aim at ensuring a full eligibility under the provisions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 but shall not aim at allowing a grandfathering of the instrument. For the case at hand, a change of the debtor or the legal format shall not per se be regarded as a material change and does not necessarily lead to the requalification as a new instrument.
According to Article 484(2) CRR, the provisions of Article 484 CRR regarding the eligibility for grandfathering of own funds instruments apply to the instrument of Bank 2 from 1 January 2014, provided that the instrument qualified as own funds under the national transposition measures for Directive 2006/48/EC on 31 December 2011.
The prevailing swap rates and credit margins on the merger date are not relevant to assess the eligibility for grandfathering or the compliance with the CRR criteria on own funds instruments.

meta.subject_matter: Grandfathering of own funds instruments

baseline.text: Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the application of grandfathering rules regarding own funds instruments is strictly tied to the specific characteristics of the instrument at the time of its initial issuance, not subsequent corporate restructuring events such as mergers. Article 484(1) CRR establishes that instruments issued prior to the entry into force of the CRR may be grandfathered provided they meet specific criteria, including the requirement that the instrument was issued in accordance with the law of the Member State at the time of issuance [CRR, Article 484(1)]. The regulatory framework does not mandate a reassessment of eligibility based on the identity of the debtor following a merger. Instead, the eligibility determination relies on the substantive features of the bond as they existed when it was originally created. Consequently, if an instrument qualified for grandfathering based on its initial terms, the change in legal entity resulting from a merger does not retroactively invalidate that status nor does it trigger a requirement to re-evaluate the instrument against current standards as if it were a new issuance. The initial characteristics of the bond remain the definitive benchmark for assessing eligibility under the grandfathering regime. This approach ensures legal certainty and prevents the erosion of capital adequacy standards through post-issuance structural changes that do not alter the fundamental nature of the debt obligation. Therefore, regulators and supervisors must assess the instrument using the parameters established at the date of its original issuance, disregarding the subsequent change in debtor status arising from the merger. This interpretation aligns with the principle that grandfathering is a transitional measure intended to recognize existing capital structures without imposing the full burden of current technical standards on instruments that were compliant under the previous regulatory environment at the time of their launch.

Article 484(1) CRR establishes that instruments issued prior to the entry into force of the CRR may be grandfathered provided they meet specific criteria, including the requirement that the instrument was issued in accordance with the law of the Member State at the time of issuance [CRR, Article 484(1)]. This approach ensures legal certainty and prevents the erosion of capital buffers due to structural changes in the banking group that occurred after the instrument's inception. question:

meta.subject_matter: Financial Conglomerates: Mismatch between ITS and DPM 3.5 – ID v22748_u - T1 L 06.00, column c0020.

baseline.text:
The discrepancy identified between the Information Transmission System (ITS) and the Data Processing Manual (DPM) 3.5 regarding Template FC.06 stems from a fundamental difference in the reporting granularity mandated by the underlying legal framework versus the technical implementation constraints. Directive 2002/87/EC (FiCOD), specifically Article 10(1), requires financial conglomerates to report risk concentrations for each individual legal entity within the group. Consequently, the supervisory reporting template FC.06 is designed to capture exposures at the legal entity level to ensure granular oversight of intra-group and external exposures. However, the DPM 3.5, which governs the technical transmission of this data, specifies that the external counterparty identification code (ID) must be unique per row. This technical limitation does not preclude the reporting of multiple exposures; rather, it necessitates that each exposure line item be associated with the specific legal entity holding that exposure.

To resolve the issue of multiple exposures towards the same external counterparty, the reporting entity must submit a separate line item for each legal entity involved. If Entity A and Entity B both hold exposures to Counterparty X, two distinct rows must be generated in the FC.06 template. The first row will contain the identification code of Entity A and the corresponding exposure amount to Counterparty X, while the second row will contain the identification code of Entity B and the exposure amount to the same Counterparty X. This approach satisfies the Directive's requirement for entity-specific reporting while adhering to the DPM's constraint on the uniqueness of the counterparty ID within a single row.

Regarding exposures denominated in different currencies, the same logic applies. The template does not aggregate amounts by currency for a single legal entity and counterparty pair. Instead, each currency denomination must be reported in a separate line item. For a single legal entity holding exposures to the same external counterparty in EUR and USD, two rows are required. The first row reports the EUR amount with the appropriate currency code, and the second row reports the USD amount. This structure ensures that the supervisory authority receives a complete picture of the risk concentration, distinguishing clearly between the legal entity, the external counterparty, and the currency denomination, thereby aligning the technical submission with the substantive requirements of FiCOD.

Directive 2002/87/EC (FiCOD), specifically Article 10(1), requires financial conglomerates to report risk concentrations for each individual legal entity within the group. Consequently, the template design necessitates that exposures be broken down by the specific legal entity holding the position. However, the DPM 3.5 specification for column c0020 allows for a single unique value for the external counterparty's identification code across all rows, which technically precludes the simultaneous reporting of multiple distinct exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies within a single submission instance.

To resolve this, the correct approach requires aggregating exposures by external counterparty at the reporting level while maintaining the entity-level breakdown in the data structure. For multiple entities holding exposures to the same external counterparty, the reporting entity must submit separate rows for each legal entity, utilizing the same counterparty ID in column c0020 for all rows corresponding to that specific counterparty. This satisfies the FiCOD requirement for entity-specific reporting while adhering to the DPM constraint of a single ID per row. Regarding exposures denominated in different currencies, the system does not support splitting a single counterparty entry into multiple rows with different currency codes under the current DPM 3.5 logic. Therefore, the reporting entity must aggregate the total exposure amount for that specific counterparty and currency combination into a single row. If multiple currencies exist for the same counterparty across the group, the entity must submit distinct rows for each currency denomination, ensuring the counterparty ID remains consistent within each currency-specific row. This methodology ensures compliance with both the Directive's substance and the DPM's technical syntax, preventing data rejection while accurately reflecting the risk concentration profile required by the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2454.

question: Is the exemption of applying strong customer authentication, in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers applicable to both payment initiation and account information services? Or, is it solely applicable to payment initiation service?
ground_truth:
Article 17 of the
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389
states that payment service providers may decide not to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) “in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers”, provided competent authorities are satisfied that the levels of security are equivalent to those provided for by Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2). This exemption applies solely to payment initiation, given it refers to “legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions”; it does not apply to account information.
Payment initiation as a process is not to be confused with payment initiation services, with the latter referring to a payment that is initiated by a third party.

meta.topic: Strong customer authentication and common and secure communication (incl. access)
meta.subject_matter: Exemption of secure corporate payment processes and protocols

baseline.text:
Under Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2), the exemption from the requirement to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) for legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions via dedicated payment processes or protocols is applicable to both the payment initiation service (PIS) and the account information service (AIS). This exemption is explicitly granted in Article 30(1)(a) of the Directive, which states that the SCA requirement does not apply to a legal person initiating a payment transaction through a dedicated payment process or protocol that is only made available to payers who are not consumers. The legislative intent behind this provision is to facilitate efficient corporate payment flows while maintaining security for non-consumer entities.

Crucially, the scope of this exemption extends beyond PIS to encompass AIS. While Article 30(1)(a) is situated within the section governing PIS, the regulatory framework and subsequent EBA/ESMA guidance clarify that the underlying principle of exempting SCA for dedicated corporate protocols applies uniformly across the relevant services where such protocols are utilized. The exemption is not limited to the act of initiating a payment but covers the broader ecosystem of secure communication and access for legal persons. Consequently, when a legal person utilizes a dedicated protocol available exclusively to non-consumer payers to access account information or initiate payments, the SCA requirement is waived for both activities. This ensures that corporate entities can operate seamlessly without the administrative burden of SCA, provided the protocol remains restricted to non-consumer users. The exemption is therefore not solely applicable to PIS but is a cross-cutting measure for dedicated corporate protocols within both PIS and AIS.

dpo.text: Under Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2), the exemption from the requirement to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) for legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions via dedicated payment processes or protocols is applicable to both the payment initiation service and the account information service, provided specific conditions are met. Article 30(1) of the Directive establishes the general obligation for providers of payment services to apply SCA for remote transactions, with limited exceptions. However, Article 30(2) explicitly carves out an exemption for legal persons acting in their own name and on their own behalf when initiating payment transactions through dedicated payment processes or protocols. Crucially, this exemption is not restricted to the payment initiation service alone; it extends to account information services where the legal person accesses information regarding their own accounts. The legislative intent, as clarified in the accompanying EBA Guidelines and ESMA Q&A documents, is to facilitate efficient corporate banking operations by recognizing that legal persons are not consumers and typically possess robust internal controls and security measures that render the consumer-focused SCA requirements disproportionate. Therefore, when a legal person utilizes a dedicated protocol available exclusively to non-consumer payers to initiate a payment or retrieve account data, the SCA requirement does not apply, aligning the regulatory treatment for both service types under the same exemption framework. This ensures a consistent approach for corporate payment flows while maintaining security for consumer-facing services.

question: Paragraphs 40) and 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees recommend that the length of the performance reference period  (if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund) should be set equal to at least 5 years. How should the performance reference period be set for the first time in light of the application date of the guidelines?
ground_truth:
[ESMA 34-43-392 UCITS Q&A, Section 11, 2a] & [ESMA 34-32-352 AIFMD Q&A, Section 15, 2]
Managers of any funds already compliant with paragraphs 40)
[1]
and 41)
[2]
of the Guidelines on performance fees before the application date of the guidelines should look at the past 5 years/whole life of the fund for the purpose of setting the performance reference period
[3]
(i.e. they should not reset the performance reference period after the application date of the guidelines).
In all the other cases, managers should apply the performance reference period starting from the beginning of the financial year following 6 months from the application date of the Guidelines (i.e. the performance reference period should start at the beginning of the financial year following 5 July 2021; by way of example, if the financial year of the fund starts on 1 September 2021, the period 1 September 2021 – 1 September 2022 should be considered as the first year of the performance reference period).
[1]
Paragraph 40) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “In case the fund employs a performance fee model based on a benchmark index, it should be ensured that any underperformance of the fund compared to the benchmark is clawed back before any performance fee becomes payable. To this purpose, the length of the performance reference period, if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund, should be set equal to at least 5 years.”
[2]
Paragraph 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “Where a fund utilises a HWM model, a performance fee should be payable only where, during the performance reference period, the new HWM exceeds the last HWM. The starting point to be considered in the calculations should be the initial offering price per share. For the HWM model, in case the performance reference period is shorter than the whole life of the fund, the performance reference period should be set equal to at least five years on a rolling basis. In this case, performance fee may only be claimed if the outperformance exceeds any underperformances during the previous five years and performance fees should not crystallise more than once a year”.
[3]
This is defined as “the time horizon over which the performance is measured and compared with that of the reference indicator, at the end of which the mechanism for the compensation for past underperformance (or negative performance) can be reset”.

meta.legal_act: Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities Directive (UCITS) Directive 2009/65/EC
meta.subject_matter: Timeline of the application of the performance reference period

baseline.text: The application of the Guidelines on performance fees, adopted under Article 10(1) of Directive 2009/65/EC, is governed by a specific transitional timeline established in Article 10(2) of the Directive itself. While the Guidelines recommend that the performance reference period be set at a minimum of five years to ensure sufficient data for meaningful risk assessment, the timing of this recommendation's application depends on the fund's status at the moment the Guidelines enter into force. For funds that are already in operation when the Guidelines become applicable, the recommendation regarding the five-year minimum period applies immediately to any new performance fee arrangements entered into thereafter. This is because the Guidelines do not mandate a retroactive adjustment of existing contractual terms but rather set standards for future conduct. Consequently, a fund manager must assess the current date against the entry-into-force date of the Guidelines. If the Guidelines were adopted on 10 December 2014, as per the Official Journal of the European Union, then for any new performance fee agreement concluded on or after that date, the reference period must be at least five years. However, for funds established prior to this date, the obligation to adhere to the five-year minimum only triggers upon the conclusion of a new performance fee arrangement post-implementation. The Guidelines explicitly state that they apply to all UCITS funds, but the practical implementation relies on the distinction between existing and new contractual engagements. Therefore, the timeline dictates that the five-year minimum is a forward-looking requirement for new agreements, ensuring that the performance reference period aligns with the regulatory intent to prevent short-termism, without imposing immediate structural changes on legacy funds unless they enter into new fee arrangements. [Directive 2009/65/EC, Article 10(2)]

dpo.text:
The application of the Guidelines on performance fees, adopted under Article 10(2) of Directive 2009/65/EC, is governed by the transitional provisions set out in Article 10(3) of the Directive itself. While the Guidelines recommend that a performance reference period shorter than the fund's life be at least five years, the timing of this recommendation's application depends on the specific lifecycle stage of the fund at the moment the Guidelines enter into force. For funds that are already in operation when the Guidelines become applicable, the recommendation regarding the five-year minimum period applies immediately to any new performance fee arrangements entered into by the fund manager. This is because the Guidelines are intended to ensure consistency and transparency in fee structures from the outset of their regulatory effect for existing schemes.

Conversely, for funds that are established after the entry into force of the Guidelines, the requirement to set the performance reference period at a minimum of five years applies from the fund's inception. The regulatory framework does not mandate a retroactive adjustment of historical performance data or existing fee structures for funds already trading prior to the Guidelines' adoption. Instead, the obligation to adhere to the five-year minimum is prospective, ensuring that new mandates and subsequent fee agreements comply with the recommended standards. This approach aligns with the general principle of legal certainty and the specific transitional mechanisms provided in the Directive to manage the shift in regulatory expectations without disrupting established financial operations. Consequently, fund managers must assess the current status of their funds against the entry date of the Guidelines to determine whether the five-year benchmark is immediately applicable or reserved for future contractual engagements.

[Directive 2009/65/EC, Article 10(3)]
[Guidelines on performance fees, Article 1]

In such case, would any general prior permission to repurchase CET 1 instruments for discretionary trading activity over treasury shares purposes result in a deduction from own funds at the time when the permission is granted or would a deduction from own funds be made at the time when the relevant repurchase of CET 1 instruments takes place?

There is no definition for “market making” in Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR). The definition of “market making activities” in Regulation (EU) No 236/2012 on short selling and certain aspects of credit default swaps is not relevant for the CRR provisions regarding the reduction of own funds and the associated provisions of Regulation (EU) No 241/2014
requirements for institutions
.
For “discretionary trading activity over treasury shares” as described in the background on the question, competent authorities may give their permission in accordance with the criteria set out in Article 78
(1)
of the

, subject to Article 29(3) of the RTS on Own Funds

) of

and

, the predetermined amount for which the competent authority has given its permission should be deducted from the moment the authorisation is granted

meta.subject_matter: Prior permission for repurchase of CET 1 instruments for discretionary trading activity over treasury shares for a certain predetermined amount.

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the repurchase of Capital Tier 1 (CET 1) instruments by a credit institution for discretionary trading activity over treasury shares constitutes a specific use of own funds that triggers the requirements of Article 78(1) last subparagraph. This provision mandates that such transactions require prior permission from the competent authority, as they involve the temporary reduction of the capital base to facilitate trading strategies that do not align with the primary purpose of holding capital for credit risk absorption. Consequently, a general prior permission granted for this specific purpose is legally required before any such repurchase can occur.

Regarding the timing of the deduction from own funds, the regulatory framework dictates that the reduction must be recognized at the moment the repurchase transaction is executed, not at the time the permission is granted. Article 78(1) last subparagraph explicitly states that the permission is subject to the condition that the repurchase does not result in a reduction of own funds below the minimum requirements applicable at the time of the transaction. Therefore, the deduction is calculated based on the actual amount of CET 1 instruments repurchased at the time of execution. If the repurchase would cause the institution's own funds to fall below the regulatory minimums at that specific point in time, the transaction is prohibited unless the institution can demonstrate that the reduction will be reversed or offset within the prescribed timeframe to restore compliance. This ensures that the capital adequacy ratio remains robust throughout the trading lifecycle, preventing temporary capital erosion that could compromise the institution's ability to absorb losses during the holding period of the treasury shares.

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the repurchase of Capital Tier 1 (CET 1) instruments by a credit institution for discretionary trading activity over treasury shares constitutes a specific use of own funds that triggers the requirements of Article 78(1) last subparagraph. This provision mandates that such transactions require prior permission from the competent authority, as they involve the temporary reduction of the capital base to facilitate trading strategies that do not align with the primary purpose of holding capital for credit risk absorption. Consequently, a general prior permission granted for this specific activity is indeed subject to the conditions laid down in Article 78(1) last subparagraph [CRR, Article 78(1) last subparagraph].

Regarding the timing of the deduction from own funds, the regulatory framework dictates that the reduction must occur at the moment the repurchase transaction is executed, not at the time the permission is granted. The logic underlying this rule is that the permission serves as a pre-authorization for the *act* of repurchasing, but the actual erosion of the CET 1 capital base only happens when the instrument is bought back from the market. Therefore, the deduction is calculated based on the nominal value of the specific CET 1 instruments repurchased at the time of the transaction. This ensures that the capital adequacy ratio reflects the real-time availability of capital after the transaction has taken place. If the permission were granted without an immediate deduction, it would create a temporary artificial inflation of the capital base, potentially misleading the competent authority and the institution regarding its true solvency position prior to the actual outflow of funds. Thus, the deduction is strictly tied to the execution date of the repurchase [CRR, Article 78(1) last subparagraph].

question: Should the ECL on debt instruments classified at fair value through OCI under IFRS9 be included within the calculation of the amount to be added back to CET1 as set in Article 473a.2 ( “static approach”)?
ground_truth:
Article 473a of the Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 establishes that, under the “static approach”, institutions are required to calculate the difference between the expected credit losses determined in accordance with paragraphs 5.5.5 and 5.5.3 of IFRS 9 at the implementation date (Article 473a(2)(b)(i)) and the amount of impairment losses determined in accordance with paragraphs 63,64, 65, 67, 68 and 70 of IAS 39 determined at 31 December 2017 or the day before the initial application of IFRS 9 (Article 473a(2)(b)(ii)). The resulting amount is the one to be considered for the application of the transitional arrangements.
The same logic, with the exclusion of credit-impaired instruments, is valid for the “dynamic approach” as established in paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 473a.
This being said, it is important to note that Article 473a does not distinguish expected credit losses recognised for instruments measured at amortised cost from expected credit losses recognised for instruments measured at fair value through other comprehensive income - FVOCI. For this reason, impairment losses on debt instruments classified as FVOCI should, therefore, be included in the calculation required by Article 473a as suggested in the alternative 1 presented by the submitter.
In addition, following the amendments introduced to Article 468 CRR, please note that the treatment of impairment losses recognised on exposures to central governments, regional governments, local authorities or public sector entities measured at FVOCI should follow the specifications under
Q&A 5346
.

meta.subject_matter: Article 473a(2) – Consideration of accounting provisions for FVOCI debt instruments

baseline.text: No, the expected credit loss (ECL) on debt instruments classified at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) under IFRS 9 must not be included within the calculation of the amount to be added back to Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) under the static approach prescribed in Article 473a(2) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013. The regulatory framework explicitly distinguishes between the accounting treatment of fair value changes and the credit risk provisioning requirements for capital adequacy purposes. While Article 473a(2) mandates that the amount to be added back to CET1 represents the difference between the accounting profit or loss and the regulatory capital impact, this calculation is strictly limited to instruments held for trading or available-for-sale where fair value changes are recognized in profit or loss. For debt instruments held at FVOCI, the ECL provision is recognized in profit or loss, but the corresponding fair value changes are routed to other comprehensive income. Consequently, the regulatory adjustment aims to neutralize the volatility of fair value movements impacting CET1, not to offset the ECL charge which is already reflected in the regulatory capital calculation via the standard ECL methodology. Including ECL in the Article 473a(2) add-back would effectively double-count the credit risk impact, as the ECL is already deducted from regulatory capital under the standard provisions of Article 473a(1) and the general ECL rules in Article 473a(2) regarding the treatment of ECL in the capital calculation. Therefore, the static approach requires the add-back to reflect only the specific fair value volatility adjustments applicable to the instrument's classification, excluding the ECL component which is handled separately under the ECL framework. This interpretation ensures that the capital buffer remains robust against credit risk without artificial inflation through the exclusion of ECL from the add-back mechanism.

dpo.text: No, the expected credit loss (ECL) on debt instruments classified at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) under IFRS 9 is not included within the calculation of the amount to be added back to Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) under the static approach set out in Article 473a(2) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013. The regulatory framework explicitly distinguishes between the accounting treatment of fair value changes and the credit risk adjustment for capital adequacy purposes. Article 473a(2) mandates that the amount added back to CET1 represents the difference between the accounting profit or loss and the regulatory profit or loss, specifically addressing the impact of fair value movements and impairment charges. However, the text of the provision limits the scope of this adjustment to the specific accounting provisions applicable to the instrument's classification. Since instruments held at FVOCI are subject to IFRS 9, the ECL provision is recorded in other comprehensive income (OCI) rather than net profit or loss. Consequently, the ECL charge does not affect the regulatory profit or loss in the manner intended by the static approach adjustment, which is designed to neutralize the impact of fair value changes recognized in profit or loss. The EBA and ESMA guidance clarify that the addition back mechanism targets the volatility introduced by fair value accounting in the income statement, not the credit risk buffer established in OCI. Therefore, including the ECL in this specific calculation would result in a double counting of the credit risk impact, as the ECL is already accounted for in the regulatory capital calculation via the specific impairment provisions in Article 473a(1) and the general capital requirements, without requiring a further addition back under the static approach. This interpretation ensures that the capital buffer reflects the true economic risk exposure without duplicating adjustments for items recorded outside the scope of the profit or loss statement.

question:
What is the treatment of a securities lending and borrowing service with regard to the LCR?
***
FR:
Quel est le traitement accordé au ratio de couverture des besoins de liquidité pour un service de prêt et d’emprunt de titres?
ground_truth:
The situation described includes two distinct transactions (lender to organisation, organization to borrower) that have to be treated separately.
From the perspective of the securities lender:
The transaction between the securities lender and the organisation is understood as being an unsecured securities lending transaction.
For the securities lender, assets lent under a securities lending and borrowing service do not meet the relevant general and operational requirements to qualify as HQLA in accordance with Articles 7 and 8 of the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. Specifically, the three day recall period is an impediment to the securities lender having ready access to its holdings of liquid assets at any time during the 30 calendar day period.
The securities lender may consider an inflow of the liquidity value corresponding to the securities lent if they are eligible to the stock of liquid assets (after being returned to the securities lender) and if the conditions of Article 32(1) are met (i.e. if they have been contractually recalled to be recovered no later than 3 business days or are contractually due within the next 30 calendar days).
From the perspective of the securities borrower:
For the securities borrower, the transaction shall be treated as a collateral swap since collateral has been provided and placed at the organisation's disposal. The securities borrowed may be included in the liquidity buffer if they meet the general and operational requirements to qualify as HQLA in accordance with Articles 7 and 8 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61.
For the calculation of cash flows, two different situations may arise and are subject to differing treatments:
Where the
liquidity value of the
securities borrowed
exceeds the liquidity value of the collateral provided
are subject to a lower haircut under Chapter 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61 than the collateral provided
, the option for the securities lender to recall its securities shall be assumed to be exercised and the securities borrower shall report an outflow
corresponding to the excess liquidity value
in accordance with Article 28(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61.
Where the
liquidity value of the
collateral provided
exceeds the liquidity value of the securities borrowed
is subject to a lower haircut under Chapter 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61 than the securities borrowed
, the securities borrower may only consider an inflow
corresponding to the excess liquidity value of the collateral lent compared to the liquidity value of the securities borrowed
if the transaction has been contractually recalled and is due within the next 30 calendar days, as provided in Article 32(3)(e) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. Otherwise, no inflow shall be reported since it would be contingent, and, under Article 32(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61, only contractual inflows maturing within 30 calendar days shall be reported as liquidity inflows in the LCR.
The liquidity value of securities or collateral mentioned above corresponds to their market value after application of the relevant haircuts in accordance with Title II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61.
In addition,
following Q&A 801
as determined in the Instructions of Part 4 on collateral swaps of Annex XXV of the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 680/2014, laying down implementing technical standards with regard to supervisory reporting of institutions according to Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council
, and in order for the borrower to determine the liquidity value of the collateral provided in a pool (at the organisation’s disposal), assets should be assumed to be encumbered in order of increasing liquidity on the basis of the liquidity classification set out in Chapter 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61, starting with assets ineligible for the liquidity buffer.
***
FR:
La situation décrite inclut deux opérations distinctes (prêteur à l’organisme, organisme à l’emprunteur) qui doivent être traitées séparément.
Du point de vue du prêteur de titres:
L’opération entre le prêteur de titres et l’organisme est considérée comme une opération de prêt de titres en blanc.
Pour le prêteur de titres, les actifs prêtés dans le cadre d’un service de prêt et d’emprunt de titres ne satisfont pas aux exigences générales et opérationnelles pertinentes pour être qualifiés d’actifs liquides de haute qualité conformément aux articles 7 et 8 du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61. Plus particulièrement, le délai de rappel de trois jours est un obstacle pour le prêteur de titres ayant aisément accès à ses avoirs d’actifs liquides à tout moment au cours de la période de 30 jours calendaires.
Le prêteur de titres peut envisager un afflux de liquidités correspondant aux titres prêtés s’ils sont éligibles au stock d’actifs liquides (après leur restitution au prêteur) et si les conditions énoncées à l’article 32, paragraphe 1, sont remplies (c’est-à-dire s’ils ont fait l’objet d’un rappel contractuel au plus tard trois jours ouvrables ou qu’ils sont contractuellement dus dans les 30 jours calendaires qui suivent).
Du point de vue de l’emprunteur de titres:
pour l’emprunteur, l’opération est traitée comme un échange de sûretés, étant donné qu’une sûreté a été fournie et mise à la disposition de l’organisme. Les titres empruntés peuvent être inclus dans le coussin de liquidité s’ils satisfont aux conditions générales et opérationnelles pour être qualifiés d’actifs liquides de haute qualité conformément aux articles 7 et 8 du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61.
Pour le calcul des flux de trésorerie, deux situations différentes peuvent se présenter et faire l’objet de traitements différents:
lorsque les
la valeur de liquidité des
titres empruntés
dépasse la valeur de liquidité de la sûreté fournie
sont soumis, en vertu du chapitre 2 du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61, à une décote inférieure à la sûreté fournie
, la possibilité pour le prêteur de rappeler ses titres est supposée exercée et l’emprunteur déclare une sortie de trésorerie
correspondant à la valeur de liquidité excédentaire
conformément à l’article 28, paragraphe 4, du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61.
Lorsque la
valeur de liquidité de la
sûreté fournie
dépasse la valeur de liquidité des titres empruntés
est soumise, en vertu du chapitre 2 du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61, à une décote inférieure aux titres empruntés
, l’emprunteur ne peut prendre en considération qu’une entrée
correspondant à la valeur de liquidité excédentaire des sûretés prêtées par rapport à la valeur de liquidité des titres empruntés
si l’opération a été rappelée par contrat et est due dans les 30 jours calendaires suivants, conformément à l’article 32, paragraphe 3, point e), du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61. Autrement, aucune entrée ne sera signalée étant donné qu’elle serait conditionnelle, et, en vertu de l’article 32, paragraphe 1, du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61, seules les entrées contractuelles arrivant à échéance dans les 30 jours calendaires seront signalées en tant qu’entrées de liquidité dans le ratio de couverture des besoins de liquidité.
La valeur de liquidité des titres ou des sûretés mentionnés ci-dessus correspond à leur valeur de marché après l’application des décotes pertinentes conformément au Titre II du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61.
En outre,
à la suite de la Q & R 801
conformément aux instructions de la partie 4 relatives aux échanges de sûretés de l’annexe XXV du règlement d’exécution (UE) nº°680/2014 de la Commission du 16 avril 2014 définissant des normes techniques d’exécution en ce qui concerne l’information prudentielle à fournir par les établissements, conformément au règlement (UE) nº 575/2013 du Parlement européen et du Conseil
, et afin que l’emprunteur détermine la valeur de liquidité de la sûreté fournie dans un panier (à la disposition de l’organisme), les actifs devraient être considérés comme étant grevés par ordre de liquidité croissante sur la base du classement de la liquidité figurant au chapitre 2 du règlement délégué (UE) 2015/61, en commençant par les actifs non admissibles dans le coussin de liquidité.

meta.subject_matter: Treatment of a securities lending and borrowing service with regard to the LCR / Traitement d’un service de prêt et d’emprunt de titres en ce qui concerne le ratio de couverture des besoins de liquidité

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, a securities lending and borrowing service is not classified as a liquidity-generating activity for the purpose of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR). Consequently, the cash inflows generated from such services are not eligible to be included in the numerator of the LCR calculation. This exclusion is explicitly mandated to ensure that the ratio reflects the institution's ability to meet its liquidity outflows over a stress period without relying on activities that do not inherently generate stable, high-quality liquid assets. The regulatory framework distinguishes between activities that create liquidity and those that merely facilitate the transfer of existing positions. Since the securities lending and borrowing service does not result in a net increase in the institution's liquid assets available to cover outflows, the cash inflows associated with these transactions are disregarded. This treatment aligns with the principle that only cash inflows from liquidity-generating activities, such as the sale of assets or the issuance of debt, may be counted. Therefore, institutions must exclude these inflows when calculating their eligible inflows. Furthermore, the cash outflows associated with the return of securities or the payment of fees related to this service are not treated as liquidity outflows for the LCR denominator, as they are considered operational costs rather than genuine liquidity drains requiring coverage by high-quality liquid assets. This specific exclusion ensures a consistent and prudent assessment of an institution's liquidity resilience, preventing the artificial inflation of the LCR through the inclusion of non-generating activities. The regulation maintains that the LCR must measure the buffer of high-quality liquid assets sufficient to survive a 30-day stress scenario, and including non-generating inflows would compromise the integrity of this stress test. Thus, the treatment remains strictly exclusionary for both inflows and outflows linked to securities lending and borrowing services.

[Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, Article 153(1)]

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, a securities lending and borrowing service is not classified as a liquidity-generating activity for the purpose of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR). Consequently, the cash inflows generated from such services are not eligible to be included in the numerator of the LCR calculation. This exclusion is explicitly stated in Article 152(1)(a) of the CRR, which defines liquidity-generating activities and lists specific types of transactions that qualify, notably excluding securities lending and borrowing. The regulatory rationale is that these services do not inherently create a net cash inflow for the institution; rather, they involve the temporary transfer of assets with a corresponding obligation to return them, often resulting in a net zero cash flow position or a liability that must be settled. Therefore, funds received from borrowers or lent to borrowers cannot be used to offset the institution's expected outflows under the LCR framework.

Furthermore, the treatment of the collateral received or provided in these transactions is governed by the specific provisions regarding eligible collateral. While the collateral itself may be eligible for the LCR if it meets the strict criteria outlined in Article 152(1)(b) and the associated technical standards, the act of lending or borrowing the securities does not generate the liquidity buffer required. The European Banking Authority (EBA) has clarified in its technical standards that the net cash flow from securities lending and borrowing is generally considered zero or negative, reinforcing the exclusion of these flows from the LCR numerator. Institutions must therefore ensure that their liquidity planning accounts for the fact that proceeds from securities lending activities cannot be relied upon to meet the 30-day stress scenario requirements of the LCR. This strict interpretation ensures that the LCR remains a robust measure of an institution's ability to survive a severe liquidity stress event without relying on activities that do not fundamentally alter its net liquidity position.

question: In EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 73 it is explained that in the calculation of the one-year default rates the number of obligors is used. Is it always mandatory to count one legal entity as one obligor, or can a group of legal entities for which there is no difference in risk due to an appropriate guarantee (i.e. those will default together) be counted as one obligor?
ground_truth:
According to Article 172(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2019/876 (CRR2), each separate legal entity to which the institution is exposed shall be separately rated. As such, the existence of a group of connected clients defined in Article 4(1)(39) CRR or the existence of third-party rating support as described in paragraph 62 of the Guidelines on PD estimation, LGD estimation and the treatment of defaulted exposures (EBA/GL/2017/16) is instead to be considered in the assignment of these separate obligors to rating grades or pools. As a matter of fact, the mere existence of an ‘appropriate guarantee’ or the existence of a rating transfer does not necessarily imply that the obligor and the third party represent a single risk with only joint defaults possible. In particular, the default status should be assessed according to the internal policies of the institution, as specified in paragraph 61 of said Guidelines, and is not necessarily automatic.
According to Article 180(1)(a) and Article 180(2)(a) CRR, institutions shall estimate PDs by obligor grade from long-run averages of one-year default rates. On this regard, Chapter 5.3 of the above mentioned Guidelines clarify the CRR requirements for the purpose of calibrating PD estimates. More in detail, for the purpose of calculating the one-year default rate referred to in Article 4(1) (78) of the CRR, paragraph 73 of the GL clarifies that the denominator “consists of the number of non-defaulted obligors with any credit obligation observed at the beginning of the one-year observation period”.
It follows that, irrespective of “the treatment of individual obligor clients and groups of connected clients” for the purpose of assigning an exposure to obligor grades or pools in accordance with Article 172(1) (d) of the CRR, each separate legal entity to which the institution is exposed constitutes an obligor for the purpose of calibrating PD estimates to the “long-run averages of one-year default rates” as defined in Article 4(1)(78) CRR.
However, where there is a significant proportion of connected obligors with a high default correlation within a considered PD model, institutions should analyse the level of risk of such obligors compared with other obligors in that model and, where necessary, reflect the difference in the level of risk in the model through appropriate risk drivers and rating criteria, for instance through different calibration segments.
In that case of high default correlation of connected obligors institutions should ensure that the lack of independence of defaults does not lead to biased results or wrong conclusions during the development or the validation of the PD model where one year default rates are computed, in particular if this high default correlation of connected obligors in the model implies a violation of the assumptions required by the underlying statistical methodologies (e.g. in the validation of model performance) in accordance with article 180(1)(d).
Please note that the differences in the treatment of unfunded credit protection and rating transfer are further clarified in
Q&A 4598
.

meta.subject_matter: Calculation of the number of obligors

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the determination of the number of obligors for calculating one-year default rates is governed by Article 127(1), which mandates that the number of obligors shall be the number of legal entities for which the credit institution has granted credit. While the EBA's guidance in EBA/GL/2017/16, paragraph 73, clarifies the methodology for deriving default rates, it does not explicitly override the fundamental definition of an obligor found in the CRR itself. Consequently, the general rule remains that each distinct legal entity constitutes a separate obligor.

However, the regulatory framework allows for aggregation under specific conditions defined in Article 127(2) of the CRR. This provision permits the treatment of a group of legal entities as a single obligor if they are part of the same group and there is no difference in risk due to an appropriate guarantee, meaning they are expected to default together. This aggregation is strictly conditional upon the existence of a "group guarantee" or a similar mechanism that ensures the entities share a common default fate. Without such a guarantee structure, the risk profile of each legal entity must be assessed independently, and they cannot be aggregated into a single obligor count.

Furthermore, the EBA's Technical Standards on Credit Risk (EBA/TS/2017/01) reinforce this distinction by detailing the criteria for identifying obligors and the specific scenarios where aggregation is permissible. The guidance emphasizes that the absence of a guarantee does not automatically preclude aggregation if other factors demonstrate identical risk, but the primary and most robust basis for combining entities remains the existence of a group guarantee. Therefore, while the CRR provides a mechanism for grouping entities with no difference in risk, the default position requires counting each legal entity individually unless the specific conditions of Article 127(2) are met. This ensures that the capital requirements accurately reflect the true exposure to default events across the portfolio.

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the determination of the number of obligors for calculating one-year default rates is governed by the principle of risk-based aggregation rather than strict legal entity boundaries. While the standard approach typically assigns one obligor per legal entity, the regulatory framework explicitly permits the aggregation of multiple legal entities into a single obligor when they exhibit identical risk profiles due to a common guarantee structure. This provision is designed to prevent the artificial inflation of default rates by treating legally distinct entities as independent risks when, in economic reality, they default simultaneously.

The specific authority for this aggregation is found in Article 127(1) of the CRR, which states that a credit institution may treat a group of legal entities as a single obligor if there is no difference in risk between them, provided that an appropriate guarantee exists ensuring their joint default. This aligns with the technical standards set out in the EBA/GL/2017/16 guidelines, where paragraph 73 clarifies that the count of obligors must reflect the actual exposure to default rather than merely the number of signatories. Consequently, if a group of legal entities is fully guaranteed by a single parent entity or a common collateral pool such that their default events are perfectly correlated, they may be counted as one obligor. This approach ensures that the resulting default rate accurately represents the probability of loss on the credit portfolio, adhering to the core objective of the Capital Requirements Regulation to measure credit risk exposure faithfully. Therefore, counting a group of legally distinct entities as one obligor is not only permissible but is often required when the risk characteristics are indistinguishable due to shared guarantees.
